content.rendered:
Ezekiel’s vision of the restored city ends not with a description of its walls but with a single, final name: The Lord Is There.

The Gospel For Today | Wednesday, August 19, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“All around shall be eighteen thousand cubits; and the name of the city from that day shall be: THE LORD IS THERE.”
Ezekiel 48:35 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

Ezekiel wrote to exiles who had lost everything that once anchored their identity: the temple destroyed, Jerusalem in ruins, the visible sign of God’s presence among them apparently gone. Chapters earlier, Ezekiel had watched in a vision as the glory of the Lord departed the temple in stages, lingering reluctantly at the threshold before withdrawing altogether (Ezekiel 10:18, 11:23) — one of the most sorrowful images in all of scripture, God’s own glory leaving the house built for Him because of the people’s persistent unfaithfulness.

But Ezekiel’s book does not end there. The final chapters describe a restored temple, a river flowing from its threshold that heals everything it touches, tribes reallocated their land, and a new city laid out in careful detail. And after all of that architecture and measurement, the book closes on a single sentence, the last words of the entire prophecy: the city’s name, from that day forward, would simply be Jehovah Shammah — the Lord is there.

Not “the Lord was there,” a memory of a glory that departed. Not “the Lord will be there,” a hope deferred to some distant future. The Lord is there — present tense, permanent, the defining feature of the city more significant than its walls or its gates or its measurements. Whatever had been lost when the glory departed in Ezekiel’s earlier vision is more than restored in this final one.

This is the trajectory of the whole Bible in miniature: a garden where God walked with man, a fall that led to exile from that presence, a tabernacle and temple where His presence returned but stayed behind a veil, a departure when the people forsook Him, and finally, in Christ, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) — God’s presence no longer housed in a building but in a Person, and through Him, in every believer who carries His Spirit. Revelation closes the whole story where Ezekiel’s vision points: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).

If you have ever felt like Ezekiel’s exiles — cut off, far from where the glory used to be, wondering if God’s presence departed along with everything else you lost — the name at the end of the story is Jehovah Shammah. Not was there. Is there. With you, right now, wherever you are reading this.

Prayer

Father, You are Jehovah Shammah, the God who is present, not distant, not departed. Where I have felt cut off or abandoned, remind me that Your presence is not tied to a place but to Your promise. Thank You that in Christ, You dwell in me by Your Spirit. You are here. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

My God is Jehovah Shammah. He is not far off. He is here, in this moment, in this place, in me by His Spirit. I am not abandoned. The Lord is there, and the Lord is here.
